doc.title: James Chirillo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Why traditional jazz is underrepresented in jazz education
summary: Opinions on why educators favor Parker and Coltrane over Bix, Duke and Louis Armstrong, and the idea that happy music seems less serious.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: We were having a discussion with a few people today about traditional jazz and they feel it’s not well represented in the jazz education scene. And I’m trying to figure out why. Why is the music of Charlie Parker and John Coltrane given more artistic weight than, you know the music of Jean Goldkette or —
Or Bix or that kind of thing.
Of course Duke, his image has been changing quite a bit I’d say over the last twenty years or so, wouldn’t you?

Even in the jazz education thing. Hmm. Well now we enter the realm of conjecture. How do I know? Am I copping a plea? I don’t know. I mean, like I say, I can conjecture. I mean I think the bottom line is simply somebody is going to teach what they feel most comfortable with and what they most like. So the generation of educators that are out there in the jazz college scene or jazz high school, whatever, those are the guys, they really, I mean maybe they listen to Duke, maybe they listen to Bix and the older guys or whatever, Louis. I mean Louis Armstrong, as far as I’m concerned, if it doesn’t come out of Louis Armstrong, it doesn’t swing, you know what I mean? I mean for me that’s what that is. And jazz now encompasses so many more influences than just a straight swing kind of thing, so it’s much arguably cerebral, whatever, you get the idea. It encompasses

a lot of other things. So whatever is going to get taught is going to get taught, it’s going to reflect the guys who are teaching it. And if that’s what they’re into, that’s what’s going to be the focus.
Sometimes I just think, when I listen to it, it’s so happy, most of it, it’s so joyous.
Yeah, it is, it’s happy music.
And sometimes I think maybe that works against it as far as being considered weighty and artistic and worth dissecting.
Because Lord knows they’ve dissected, you know, almost every other kind of jazz.

That’s right, I know. It’s almost as if it’s an accepted corollary that if it’s happy stuff then it can’t be that serious. It’s not serious. And again, as far as I’m concerned if Louis Armstrong did it that’s serious enough for me. If Duke Ellington did it, that’s serious enough for me. If Red Allen did it, that’s serious — Jack Teagarden, and the list just goes on and on and on. And those guys, those were the guys that defined everything that we’re doing today. Those were the guys who John Coltrane and Cannonball and Johnny Hodges, who was Cannonball listening to? Willie Smith, Benny Carter, Johnny Hodges, who was he listening to?
I thought of that yesterday when I had this recording of him doing “Stars Fell on Alabama” [scats] just like Johnny Hodges.
